summary: A 1980 specification of the File Transfer Protocol, for moving files between hosts. It replaced RFC 542 and was replaced by RFC 959.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 765 describes FTP as a protocol with one connection for commands and replies and another for file data. It lets the parties choose how data is represented and transferred, and it was later replaced by RFC 959.

subtitle: An FTP specification with separate control and data connections.

tldr.problem: Hosts need a common way to transfer files despite differences in their storage systems and data representations.
tldr.mechanism: FTP uses a TELNET control connection for commands and replies and a separate data connection for files, with settings for representation, structure, and transfer mode.
tldr.outcome: RFC 765 replaced RFC 542 and was later obsoleted by RFC 959.

today: RFC 765 replaced RFC 542 and has been obsoleted by RFC 959.

sections.title: Control and Data Connections
sections.content:
FTP separates control from file transfer. A TELNET connection carries commands from the user's protocol interpreter to the server's interpreter and carries replies back. A separate data connection carries file contents between data transfer processes.

The data connection may connect the user and server or two servers. The control connections stay open while data transfer is in progress, and the data connection need not exist all the time.
sections.plainLanguage: Commands and replies travel over a control connection. The file itself travels over a separate data connection.

sections.title: Representation, Structure, and Mode
sections.content:
FTP transfer settings describe different things. The representation type describes data, such as ASCII, EBCDIC, Image, or Local byte. The file structure can be File, Record, or Page. The transfer mode can be Stream, Block, or Compressed. The defaults are ASCII Non-print, File structure, and Stream mode.

Transfer bytes are always 8 bits, even when the logical byte size used to interpret a file differs. The RFC says files should be stored and retrieved with the same parameters to preserve their original form.
sections.plainLanguage: The parties choose how to interpret the file, whether it has records or pages, and how to send it. These settings help hosts with different internal formats exchange data.

sections.title: Commands and File Operations
sections.content:
Commands identify the user, set transfer parameters, and request file operations. Examples include USER and PASS for access control, TYPE and MODE for transfer settings, and RETR, STOR, and APPE for retrieving, storing, and appending files. The server returns replies over the control connection.

Pathnames follow the server site's conventions. The RFC notes that password information is sensitive and assigns the user-FTP process responsibility for hiding it from display.
sections.plainLanguage: The user sends commands to log in, choose transfer settings, and request file actions. The server replies with a numeric code and text describing the result.

sections.title: Replies, Errors, and Restart
sections.content:
Every command must receive at least one reply. A reply begins with a three-digit code used by programs to determine the next state, followed by text intended for people. The first digit indicates whether the action is starting, complete, awaiting more information, temporarily unsuccessful, or permanently unsuccessful.

Block and Compressed modes support restart markers for recovery after major system failures. The RFC assigns detection of lost or scrambled bits during transfer to TCP rather than FTP.
sections.plainLanguage: Reply codes tell the client whether an action succeeded, failed, or needs more information. Restart markers can help resume some transfers after a system failure.
